name: Philipp Schmid
bio: Philipp Schmid is a Staff Engineer at Google DeepMind working on Gemini and Gemma. His work focuses on helping developers build and benefit from AI responsibly.

sessions.scheduled_title: Why Agents Should Have Their Own Sandbox

positions.claim: Human-written skills outperform AI-generated skills, and AI-generated skills can degrade performance.
A skills.md file should be under 500 lines.
Skills improve agent performance by roughly 15% on average, per Skill Bench 1.1 across ~100 tasks.
If a workflow is a fixed sequence of steps, it should be a script rather than a skill.
Most skill evals can be cheap regex assertions rather than LLM-as-judge.
About 50% of skill failures come from the skill not being triggered, not from bad skill content.
Evals should measure task outcomes, not whether the skill was loaded on a particular turn.
Skill evals must run in isolated workspaces because coding agents will otherwise cheat by reading prior chats or executions.
You should run three to six trials per eval case because agents are non-deterministic.
Skills should be tested across multiple agent harnesses, since a skill that works on one harness may fail on another.
A skill change should not be merged unless it improves the eval test cases.
Evals should be retained after a skill is retired, serving as regression tests that signal when to reintroduce it.
User-invoked skills are underrated and are the right fit for routine dev workflows like creating pull requests or staging documentation.
Skill descriptions should include negative cases specifying when not to use the skill, to prevent over-triggering.
Removing no-ops from skills saves tokens even when it does not change eval performance.
Capability skills are temporary and will be obsoleted by better models, while preference skills are durable.
